name: PT Garuda Maintenance Facility Aero Asia Tbk

frontmatter.title: GMF AeroAsia - the dilution is behind it, the cash conversion is not
frontmatter.summary: A state-controlled aircraft maintenance franchise that has been recapitalised, priced as if the recapitalisation never happened. The rights issue now filed adds a sixth more shares at a price below our value; we have trimmed the target for that dilution, but the balance sheet is still fixed and the next test is converting group work into cash.
thesis: The price fall overstates the value destruction - the share count multiplied through the land-inbreng rights issue completed in January 2026, so the per-share fall is mostly new shares, and equity value fell about a quarter from its high, not by the share-price decline.
Affiliate work from Garuda Group is the bulk of revenue and the parent is being recapitalised, so the revenue base is more secure than the tiny free float and the penny price suggest.

EBITDA is company-reported at a level the market is capitalising at a deep discount, and capex is a fraction of what an asset-heavy MRO would normally spend because the hangar land arrived by inbreng.
Net debt falls on our forecasts as free cash flow is applied to debt, and the payout policy is now legally possible after the retained-deficit clean-up.
The state's own November 2026 transfer valued the whole company far above the market price.

catalysts.event: Oman GMF Technic, the joint venture with Oman Air, starts full operations
FY2026 audited results against the company's own revenue and net profit targets
RUPSLB to approve the free-float rights issue - share count, nominal price and proceeds now filed with the exchange
Listing and effective date of the rights issue shares, and the resulting free-float position
Completion of Garuda's rights issue, which puts the controlling stake back under Garuda

blocks.text: **What changed since publication.** GMF filed the terms of the free-float rights issue that the initiation could only describe as a flag: up to 22,030 million new Series B shares at a nominal of Rp19 each, targeting US$59.4m of gross proceeds, to be voted at a RUPSLB on 19 November 2026 [S12][S13]. The issue is 17.6% of the current count and 15.0% of the enlarged one, and the proceeds imply an issue price about a seventh above today's Rp42 and less than half the value we put on the share. That is a transfer from holders who do not subscribe to the new money, so the dilution line in the bridge moves from a flagged probability to a near-certain one and the target trims to Rp122. The move is small relative to the size of the issue because the initiation already carried a probability-weighted version of the same deduction in the bridge; the filing raises both the likelihood and the dollar size of the item, and that delta - not the issue itself - is what the target now reflects. What the filing also adds is the pro forma, which delevers. Nothing in the operating forecast changes, the company's own pro forma shows the balance sheet improving rather than straining, and the rating is unchanged.

BUY with a twelve-month target of Rp122, 190.9% total return from Rp42 [S0]. GMF AeroAsia is the Indonesian aircraft maintenance, repair and overhaul incumbent: it maintains airframes, engines, components and landing gear for Garuda Indonesia, Citilink, the defence fleet and third-party airlines from its hangars at Soekarno-Hatta [S7]. The company earned US$491.9m of revenue and US$79.9m of EBITDA in FY2025 [S4], and reported US$413.4m of revenue and US$57.4m of EBITDA in the nine months to September 2026, both well up on the same period a year earlier [S3].

The variant view is about what the share price is measuring. The shares fell from a twelve‑month high of Rp151 [S0] to Rp42, but the share count went from 47,386 million at end‑2024 to 124,836 million today after the land‑inbreng rights issue completed on 27 January 2026 [S0][S7 p.22]. The arithmetic: at the twelve‑month high on the old count the equity was capitalised above today's IDR5,243.1bn market capitalisation [S0], so the fall in equity value is far smaller than the per‑share price decline. Most of the per‑share fall is the multiplication of the share count, not a smaller business. What the market is now pricing is not a smaller company but a permanently impaired one: 7.2x FY2026E EV/EBITDA, 8.1x P/E and a 10.7% FCFE yield. That is a price for stagnation and a governance discount, not for a business earning 14.2% EBITDA margins with falling net debt.

Three things move the value. First, the revenue path. Affiliate work is US$340.0m of US$491.9m FY2025 revenue and depends on Garuda Group's fleet reactivation [S7][S6]. Second, cash conversion: operating cash flow through September was a fraction of US$22.1m of net profit, because receivables absorbed the growth [S0]. Third, the discount rate and the dilution overhang: the free-float rights issue is now sized and priced, with the cash arriving in exchange for new shares at a price well below our value [S12]. We hold all three at the most probable path, not the safest one: revenue at the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter no larger than last year's, costs at the rates the audited accounts actually show, working capital at the last actual rather than an assumed release, and no new shares in the forecast count until the issue is effective - it is carried as a probability-weighted dilution item in the bridge, which is the same arithmetic as issuing the shares and adding the cash, done in one place.

GMF AeroAsia is a 5,205-person MRO provider based at Soekarno-Hatta International Airport, Tangerang [S0]. It reports three revenue segments: repair and overhaul, which was 79.3% of FY2025 revenue at US$390.0m; line maintenance, the daily and transit checks that shrank in FY2025; and other operations including defence and industrial services [S7]. The revenue mix is concentrated by customer rather than by service: Garuda Group affiliates supplied US$340.0m of FY2025 revenue against US$126.0m from non-affiliates, so roughly seven rupiah in ten come from companies under the same ultimate control [S7]. Commercial aviation was 75.4% of first-quarter 2026 revenue, the segment that carries the growth [S4].

The capability set is the moat argument. During 2025 the company added B737 MAX and B787 platform capability plus landing gear and aero-structure work, and it holds the certifications that let it serve foreign carriers [S7]. The hangars sit inside Indonesia's busiest airport, which is a real locational advantage for domestic airlines and a real constraint on growth: heavy maintenance capacity is fixed, so revenue growth has to come from higher utilisation and higher-value work rather than from new bays. The defence and engine shops diversify away from the civil aviation cycle [S7].

Growth beyond the home base is now explicit. In November 2026 GMF and Oman Air inaugurated Oman GMF Technic, an even-split joint venture at Muscat International Airport with two hangars, wide-body and narrow-body capacity, an adjustable docking system and a revenue target of US$44.0m a year from January 2027 [S5]. Because it is a joint venture its revenue is not consolidated; its value to GMFI is equity income plus the option on Middle East work, and we do not put its revenue in our consolidated line [S5].

Ownership has been rebuilt twice in two years. Garuda Indonesia began 2025 holding almost all of the company; during the year Angkasa Pura Indonesia took 65.8% through a non-cash rights issue in which land was contributed, leaving Garuda with a minority and the public with a sliver [S7]. In November 2026 Angkasa Pura transferred that stake to InJourney as a dividend in specie [S10], and Garuda's rights issue is designed to take it back through an inbreng from Danantara Asset Management [S6]. The direction of travel is a single aviation group under Danantara, with GMFI as its maintenance arm. That is strategically coherent and a governance concentration at the same time.

The global MRO market is forecast to grow at 2.8% a year to reach USD157bn by 2035, according to the Oliver Wyman forecast the company cites in its 2025 report [S7]. Indonesia should outgrow that: the domestic fleet is expanding, Garuda is reactivating aircraft, and regional maintenance capacity is short after years of under-investment. The binding constraint in 2025 was the supply chain - limited production capacity and late deliveries of materials and spare parts meant demand exceeded available supply, which is simultaneously a revenue ceiling and a margin problem [S7]. That constraint is the single best explanation of why a company with a captive customer base still reported a gross margin in the high teens for most of 2026 rather than the low twenties it earned in the good quarters of 2025 [S7].

Competition is national and regional. Domestically GMF is the incumbent with the only heavy-maintenance footprint at scale, which gives it a natural advantage for Indonesian carriers who do not want to fly aircraft abroad for checks. Regionally it competes with Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and the Gulf for third-party work, where price, turnaround time and certification decide. The company's own disclosure splits the market into affiliate and non-affiliate revenue because the two behave differently: affiliate work is contracted within the group, while non-affiliate work is won against regional MROs on commercial terms [S7]. The Oman joint venture is an attempt to compete in the Gulf on the Gulf's terms rather than exporting from Jakarta, and to qualify for the certifications that open that market [S5].

Five forces, in order of severity. Buyer power is high: a handful of airlines, with the controlling shareholder's own carriers taking most of the revenue, so pricing is negotiated inside a group rather than discovered in a market [S7]. Supplier power is high and rising: components and materials are scarce, and subcontracting is now the largest purchased input, having grown faster than revenue in FY2025 as engine work increased [S7]. Barriers to entry are moderately high - certifications, hangars and licensed engineers - which is why the franchise has lasted seven decades and why new capacity in Indonesia is slow to appear. Substitutes are limited for heavy checks; line maintenance is more contestable and is the segment that shrank. Rivalry is regional rather than local, so GMF's pricing is set by what a Singapore or Gulf shop would charge, adjusted for the inconvenience of the customer's aircraft being away longer.

The moat is therefore real but narrow: location, certifications and a captive customer base. It does not confer pricing power against that customer base, and the evidence is a gross margin that has moved with the supply-chain cycle rather than ratcheting upward [S7]. A narrow moat sets the fade assumption in the valuation section more than the growth assumption does: we assume the company holds share and earns a normal return on capital, not that it expands margins beyond its last good year.

The regulatory frame is permissive rather than restrictive. Maintenance organisations operate under civil-aviation approved maintenance organisation rules, and the company's ability to serve foreign carriers depends on holding the relevant approvals from the United States and European authorities as well as the local regulator [S7]. The Oman venture is pursuing the same approvals, which is the gate that determines whether a Gulf hangar can serve Western fleets [S5]. For GMFI the practical regulatory risk is certification loss or suspension, which would be severe but is not a live issue today.

Aircraft heavy maintenance is a schedule-driven business: airframes come due for major checks at fixed
intervals, so an MRO's revenue is a function of the fleet's age and flight hours, not of the airline
cycle alone. That gives visibility but also means that a fleet reactivation delay moves revenue by
quarters, and that capacity, once built, is sticky. Airlines typically keep a primary and a backup
maintenance provider for each fleet type, so a shop that loses an approval loses the whole allocation,
not a share of it.

Revenue grew from US$238.7m in FY2022 to US$491.9m in FY2025 as Indonesian aviation recovered from the pandemic, more than doubling over three years [S7]. Operating income rose from US$42.0m to US$60.6m over the two audited years and net profit attributable to shareholders to US$33.9m [S11]. The nine-month 2026 figures are US$413.4m of revenue, US$57.4m of EBITDA and US$22.1m of net profit [S3].

Two corrections to the data pack matter. First, the pack overstates FY2025 operating income; the audited accounts report operating income of US$60.6m on total operating expenses of US$431.3m, against the US$42.0m and smaller expense block the pack carries for the prior year [S11]. We restate FY2024 and FY2025 revenue, operating income, D&A, net profit and capex from the filing, and the model rebuilds EBITDA from them: US$79.9m against the US$80.2m management reported [S4]. Second, the pack's D&A line is incomplete in FY2025; the notes give US$19.3m for FY2025 against US$18.7m for FY2024, and those are the figures the model uses [S11]. Without that restatement the model would carry a cash-cost base that is too high and an EBITDA that is too low. We confine our historical claims to the two restated years: the audited five-year summary does show positive operating income in FY2022 and FY2023, but its thousands-separated columns are not machine-readable in the archive, so pre-2024 levels in the model's history table are the pack's and we do not quote them [S7 p.18].

Margins are the heart of the forecast, and the honest place to start is that GMFI does not report a gross profit. The audited consolidated income statement runs revenue of US$491.9m straight into a single operating-expense block of US$431.3m - employee expenses [F32], materials [F33], subcontract [F34], depreciation [F8], operational expenses [F35] and other operating expenses [F36] - and then to operating income of US$60.6m [S11 p.18]. There is no Pokok Pendapatan line anywhere in the filing. Every "gross margin" this house prints for GMFI, including the nine-month figure that used to anchor this section, is therefore a derived split, not a filing fact: the pack allocates the operating-expense block into cost of revenue and SG&A, and that allocation is a vendor construct with no Q3-2026 LK behind it - the company's investor-relations page still ends at the 30 June 2026 interim [S2].

We now run the model on the audited basis and say so. Cost of revenue is the four direct production lines the notes disclose; SG&A is the two remaining audited lines. On FY2025 that split reproduces the audited operating income exactly, at a gross margin in the high teens and 7.7% of SG&A. The FY2026E margin is then derived from the only 2026 figure that is sourced - nine-month EBITDA of US$57.4m on US$413.4m of revenue [S3] - with D&A at 3.9% and SG&A at the audited rate, giving 17.8%. That is lower than the FY2025 level because the nine-month actual is lower, and it gives the December quarter no margin above the FY2025 peak: the fourth quarter at the nine-month margin is exactly what the model assumes.

Revenue follows the same discipline. Nine months are actual [S3][S8] and the fourth quarter is US$491.9m less the nine-month figure of last year - that is, no growth on the FY2025 December quarter and no seasonal uplift - which gives US$598.2m, about a tenth above the company's own US$542.8m target [S4]. That ratio is not a stretch: FY2025 revenue landed a tenth above the target the company set for it, and profit a quarter above [S7 p.32]. The June target, taken literally, would require a December quarter a third smaller than the one a year earlier, in the quarter the accounts show as the largest of the year, with nothing in the reactivation or contract disclosure to explain it.

Capex is the most unusual line in the model. Cash capex was US$4.6m in FY2025 and US$4.2m in FY2024, under one per cent of revenue, because the land under the hangars came in by inbreng rather than purchase [S7]. We lift it to 1.2% of revenue in FY2026E and 1.5% in FY2027E to fund the platform capabilities and the Oman venture, which is still an asset-light number for an MRO and is a key reason free cash flow is large relative to the market capitalisation [S5]. If capex instead normalises toward the depreciation charge, the cash-flow case weakens materially - that is one of our signposts.

Working capital is where the earnings-quality question sits. Operating working capital was US$-18.1m at end-2025 and turned positive by September 2026 as receivables rose to about two months of revenue, concentrated in Garuda and Citilink [S0][S8]. Operating cash flow through September was a fraction of net profit [S0]. The earnings-quality screen is run on the three-year numbers, not asserted: net profit less operating cash flow over average total assets was negative in two of the last three years and single-digit throughout, receivables grew slower than revenue over those three years, and the cash conversion of the first nine months of 2026 is the one number that has broken down - the calculation is set out line by line in the assumptions file so a reader can rebuild it. Cash conversion, not the accruals level, is the flag: the counterparty is the controlling shareholder, and a receivable that does not collect is an impairment, not a timing difference. That is why the bear case writes off a sixth of the receivable book rather than only stretching working capital.

The balance sheet was rebuilt. Equity went from US$-258.1m at end-2024 to US$114.4m at end-2025 after the land inbreng [S0], gross debt fell to US$384.8m and net debt to US$343.7m [S0]. On our forecasts net debt falls to US$255.3m in FY2027E and US$77.5m by FY2030E, which is 0.7x EBITDA, because free cash flow is applied to debt rather than to acquisitions [S7]. The rights issue accelerates that on the company's own full take-up pro forma: cash goes to US$101.8m and the liabilities-to-equity ratio to 3.3x, so part of the deleveraging the forecast takes years to deliver arrives in one step [S12][S13]. Capital allocation is therefore simple: deleverage, then distribute. The policy cap is 30.0% of profit and nothing has been paid since listing, and the balance sheet still carried an unappropriated accumulated deficit of US$523.1m at 31 December 2025 [S11 p.17]. The quasi-reorganisation that would clear it appears in the 2025 report as a plan put to the board committee in December 2025, not as a completed transaction [S7 p.272]. One dividend path therefore runs through this report: zero payout in FY2026E because no distribution can be declared against that deficit, then the full 30.0% cap from FY2027E. The template pays a year's declared dividend in the following year, which is why FY2026E dividends paid are zero and the target carries no next-twelve-month DPS.

A note on the shape of the forecast [S7]. FY2026E is nearly a reported year: nine months are actual and the fourth quarter is the company's own target. FY2027E is the first genuinely uncertain year, because it combines the completion of Garuda's reactivation with the start of the Oman joint venture. We grow revenue 9.0% that year and fade the rate to 5.0% by FY2030E, which is above the global market rate because Indonesia starts from a lower base, then 5.0% from FY2031E onward. The terminal growth in the DCF is lower still, at 2.5%, and the fade to it is deliberate: the explicit forecast carries the volume leverage, the perpetuity carries almost none.

We value GMFI on a ten-year FCFF discounted-cash-flow model, weighted entirely to that method. The choice is deliberate. There is no listed Indonesian MRO peer, and the company's own multiple history is unusable: the share count changed from 47,386 million to 124,836 million against a negative equity base, so the historical P/E and P/BV series mix two different companies and a meaningless per-share denominator. A peer median drawn from shipping and airline names would import a trough multiple onto a business at a trough margin, which is the error we are trying to avoid rather than repeat. The multiple tables below are shown as cross-checks only; they carry no weight in the target.

The discount rate is the engine's Indonesian build, and here is the arithmetic rather than a reference to it. The risk-free rate is 5.1%, the mature-market equity premium 4.2% and the country premium 2.5%. The unlevered beta of 0.90 is the industry regression; levered at the market debt-to-equity of 1.24 it is 1.77. The cost of equity applies the beta to the sum of the equity premium and the country premium - 5.1% plus 1.77 times (4.2% plus 2.5%) - giving 17.0%. Debt is priced at 7.1% pre-tax, which is the risk-free rate plus the corporate spread, at a 22.0% marginal rate; with equity at 44.6% and debt at 55.4% the WACC is 10.6%.

Two things worth having out in the open. First, the country premium is scaled by the levered beta in that formula. The additive form - the premium added once, unscaled - would give a cost of equity about two points lower and, at the same weights, a WACC near the top of the house band for USD names. We keep the scaled form because it is the engine's house build and because it is the more conservative of the two: the grid below shows what the value does at a WACC one point lower, so the reader can see how much of the target depends on the choice. It is not a defence of a high rate at any price - it is a statement that a small-cap MRO with related-party revenue, a 6.5% float and dollar debt against a thin equity base should not be discounted at the bottom of the band. Second, the model charges interest at 5.0%, the observed FY2025 rate on the debt actually outstanding, while the WACC uses 7.1%, the marginal cost of new debt. The two are consistent by design: the interest line prices the balance sheet as it is, the discount rate prices cash flows that would be financed at today's spread.

The DCF produces an enterprise value of US$1,080.1m for the operating business, of which the terminal value is 50.8%, and a value per share of Rp105 [S0]. That is the DCF value. Rolled twelve months forward at the cost of equity it becomes the base scenario, Rp123, and the probability-weighted blend of the three scenarios set out in section five is the Rp122 target. One chain, three numbers: DCF, base case, weighted target.

The rights issue is the one capital event between the balance sheet and the target, and it is carried in the bridge rather than in the forecast share count. The company proposes 22,030 million new Series B shares - 17.6% of the current count - for US$59.4m of gross proceeds, which implies an issue price about a seventh above today's Rp42 and less than half the Rp105 we put on a share [S12][S13]. The arithmetic is done once, in the bridge: a holder who takes up the rights is neither better nor worse off, a holder who does not is diluted by the difference, and the probability-weighted deduction is that difference. Had the issue been struck at intrinsic value the deduction would vanish; at a deeper discount it would be larger. The company's own pro forma, on full take-up, takes cash to US$101.8m, total equity to US$204.0m and total assets to US$885.9m, and cuts its liabilities-to-equity ratio to 3.3x [S12][S13]. That is the company's arithmetic rather than ours, and it is why we do not read the issue as a solvency event: it is a free-float fix that happens to delever.

The multiple-survival test is the check that matters here, and it is run, not asserted. The terminal value is struck on FY2035E EBITDA of US$138.3m [S0] at an implied exit multiple a little under ten times. The entry is 7.2x FY2026E EV/EBITDA at Rp42 today, so the exit sits about four-tenths above entry - a real expansion, not a rounding difference, and the 50.8% of enterprise value the terminal value carries says how much of the target rests on it. We disclose it rather than bury it inside the enterprise value. The defence is not that the market price is wrong in the abstract: the entry multiple is depressed by a rock-bottom float, a rights issue struck below intrinsic value and a controlling-shareholder overhang that the exit year does not have. The harder anchor is the state's own November 2026 transaction, in which Angkasa Pura transferred 65.8% of GMFI to InJourney for IDR5.66tn [S10]: on our FY2026E EBITDA that implies about nine and a third times for the whole of the company - between the market's entry multiple and our implied exit, and paid by informed owners within the last fortnight. If a buyer paid only the entry multiple at exit, the DCF value per share would fall by about a fifth; that is the size of the multiple bet, and it is a fifth we accept on the transfer anchor, not one we leave the reader to discover.

We reject weighting transport‑services peers because an MRO franchise is not a shipping company; embedding their trough multiples in the target would import a structural discount where none existed before. We disclose the peer‑median data,
, as the datum a precedent‑multiple buyer would anchor on, and accept the divergence.

**The state valuation anchors.** On 2 November 2026 Angkasa Pura transferred 65.8% of GMFI to InJourney for IDR5.66tn [S10]. Dividing the stake value by the stake gives a value for the whole company that sits between the market's 7.2x entry and the implied exit multiple in the DCF. The state's own transaction, even if negotiated between two related entities, establishes that informed owners paid far above the market price, and that reality is the anchor around which the terminal-multiple bet is sized.

**Translation risk.** GMFI's revenue is mostly affiliate work billed in dollars inside the Garuda Group, but Garuda's own accounts are IDR-denominated, and the house macro deck moves the rupiah from 18,190 to 18,600 by FY2028E, a steady weakening. The USD-reported forecast therefore embeds a translation gain on dollar revenue but a translation loss on the rupiah cost base and on the rupiah-denominated debt service; the net is roughly neutral at the revenue line but the balance-sheet channel is exposed, because gross debt of US$384.8m against equity of US$114.4m means a rupiah drop hits the equity disproportionately. The rights-issue proceeds – US$59.4m translated at 18,190 – convert to fewer dollars if the rupiah weakens, which shrinks the cash leg of the pro forma and changes the dilution arithmetic. A materially weaker rupiah cuts the dollar value of those proceeds and enlarges the dilution deduction proportionally; we disclose that as a risk and keep the macro deck's central path in the base case rather than modelling a depreciation that is not the central projection.

The cross-checks disagree in an informative way. At Rp42 the market pays 7.2x FY2026E EV/EBITDA, 8.1x P/E, 1.9x P/BV and gets a 10.7% FCFE yield, rising to 20.0% next year. Our DCF value per share is Rp123 against a market capitalisation of IDR5,243.1bn [S0]. Between the two sits the most useful third data point: in November 2026 Angkasa Pura transferred 65.8% of GMFI to InJourney for IDR5.66tn, which values the whole company far above the market price and below our DCF [S10]. The state's own transaction price is an administered, related-party number, so it is neither fair value nor a floor; it is evidence that the market price is not the price informed owners put on the asset.

What today's price implies is now a solver output, not an inference. Holding the discount rate and the margin path, the engine's reverse-DCF solver on FY2027E revenue growth says today's Rp42 is consistent with revenue growth -7.1% below our base in that year and every year after - not a slower recovery but a franchise that shrinks relative to the recovery already visible in the nine-month actual. We also read the implication off the multiples: a 10.7% FCFE yield on a company with net debt of 3.7x EBITDA falling to 0.7x and no maturity wall is pricing governance and dilution risk, not solvency risk. We think the market is right to charge something for those risks and wrong to charge this much.

Sensitivity is concentrated in three inputs: revenue growth, gross margin and the discount rate. A two point change in revenue growth moves the value by roughly a tenth, a one point change in gross margin by a similar amount, and a one point change in WACC by about as much again. The rating survives a one-point higher WACC and a one-point lower margin at the same time, which is the test we care about; it does not survive a permanent step down in the gross margin to the nine-month 2026 level.

**Related-party dependence - likelihood high, impact high.** US$340.0m of US$491.9m FY2025 revenue came from Garuda Group affiliates, and Garuda itself is loss-making and raising equity [S7][S8]. A parent that pays late transfers its own liquidity problem to GMFI's receivables, which already stand at about two months of revenue [S0]. This is the risk that most deserves the discount the market is applying, and it is the one we cannot diversify away inside the position.

**Dilution and free float - likelihood high, impact medium.** The public holds a sliver of the shares and the free float is 6.5%, below the exchange requirement; the rights issue now has a ratio, a nominal price and a vote date - 22,030 million new shares at Rp19 nominal for US$59.4m, before the RUPSLB on 19 November 2026 [S12][S13]. We do not wave it away as value-neutral. Issuing a sixth more shares at a price near today's market - less than half the DCF value per share - transfers value from holders who do not subscribe to the new money, which is why the base case carries a probability-weighted bridge deduction, and why the bear case has the issue only partly taken up. Two things we cannot yet source: whether the controlling holder takes up its 65.8% entitlement, which decides whether the float is actually fixed, and the timetable from approval to listing. If the issue is priced at or above intrinsic it is accretive and the deduction reverses; the disclosure implies a price above the market but far below our value, so the deduction stands. There is also a governance tail the dilution line does not capture: if the RUPSLB rejects the issue, the free float stays below the exchange minimum and the non-compliance overhang outlives the vote [S12][S13].

**Currency - likelihood medium, impact medium.** Gross debt of US$384.8m against equity of US$114.4m means a rupiah move hits the equity disproportionately, and the house macro deck has the rupiah at 18,350 by FY2027E and 18,600 by FY2028E. The nine-month result already shows the transmission: net profit of US$22.1m was held back by an exchange loss as the rupiah weakened [S3], even though the revenue is dollar-denominated and the company hedges [S7]. The balance sheet and the rights-issue proceeds are the two channels; both move against us in a weaker-rupiah world.

**Operational - likelihood medium, impact medium.** Heavy maintenance is concentrated at a single airport, supply-chain delays for parts recur, and the subcontract line is the first thing to inflate when the supply chain tightens [S7]. The Oman joint venture adds execution risk in a new jurisdiction from January 2027, and an even-split structure means GMFI does not control it [S5].

**Liquidity and float - likelihood medium, impact high.** Three-month average daily turnover is IDR5.1bn on a 6.5% float, so an institutional position cannot be built or exited quickly [S0]. The float figure is the IDX registry measure carried in the data pack, and it is far below the exchange's free-float requirement - which is the stated reason for the rights issue now in front of shareholders [S12]. On the exchange status the earnings-quality card requires us to check: the name is not on the special-monitoring board in the registry mirror we can see [S0], and we found no B, E, L, M or S notation disclosure in the filings we archived [S11]. That is a check, not a clearance. If the name were moved to the special-monitoring board the consequence would be full call auction, which would break the entry and exit assumptions outright on a float this thin, and no liquidity discount can fix that. We apply no liquidity discount because turnover is above the house threshold [S0], but we size the position against the float, not the market capitalisation: at this float a position of any institutional size is a governance bet with an exit problem attached.

The bear case has Garuda's restructuring stalling, affiliate revenue slipping, a sixth of the receivable book written off under PSAK 71, the rights issue landing at a discount and working capital absorbing cash; its twelve-month value is Rp69. The bull case has the reactivation accelerating, Oman ramping and margin leverage, worth Rp200; the base is Rp123. The probabilities are 50.0% base, 30.0% bear and 20.0% bull, and those three values weight to the Rp122 target in the investment summary - the same run, the same tokens, no separate arithmetic. The two tails shock the same four drivers by mirrored amounts.

The bear's write‑off of about a sixth of the net receivable book is anchored in the audited note, not assumed. Gross trade receivables were US$185.2m, already more than half provided at US$107.0m, with US$86.7m more than a year past due – nearly half the gross book – and the related‑party gross book of US$108.3m carried at a provision of US$40.8m [S11 Note 5]. A further sixth of the NET book is therefore a step in the existing ECL matrix, not a new assumption. Two things the bear also carries that a pure earnings shock misses: a two‑point rise in GMFI's own cost of debt as Garuda's stalled recapitalisation widens the group's spread, and the risk that the 19 November 2026 RUPSLB rejects the free‑float rights issue outright, in which case the float stays below the exchange minimum and the non‑compliance overhang outlives the dilution [S12][S13]. On the bull side, the upside is not only faster revenue: a reversion of working capital to the FY2025 negative position releases cash, and Oman GMF Technic success lifts the non‑affiliate revenue share, which is the one variable that can compress the related‑party discount in the cost of equity rather than just add earnings [S5]. At a mid‑point probability and a conservative multiple the JV item is worth less than the base‑case bridge by a margin that is a rounding error against the target, and we disclose it rather than hide it.

Signposts that would change our view: a quarterly decline in affiliate revenue; receivables days moving above three months or a PSAK 71 charge in a quarterly filing; a rights issue priced below the prevailing market price; the loss of a major third-party or defence contract; and any change in the dividend policy before the FY2026 results.

Ownership is the defining feature. A 65.8% controlling stake sat with Angkasa Pura at the end of FY2025, with Garuda holding a minority and the public a sliver [S7]; in November 2026 that block moved to InJourney as a dividend in specie [S10] and is destined for Garuda through the Danantara inbreng [S6]. The practical consequence is that GMFI's customer, supplier of capital and controlling shareholder are the same group. Related-party revenue of US$340.0m on US$491.9m of revenue is the number to hold in mind when reading any margin: group pricing can move value between GMFI and its parent without a visible transaction, and the auditor's related-party note is the only place it appears.

The free float is 6.5% [S0], below the exchange minimum, and closing that gap is the stated reason for the rights issue filed on 13 November 2026 [S12]. Whether it closes depends on take-up, which the disclosure does not settle: if the controlling holder subscribes its 65.8% share the public's proportion is unchanged and the float problem survives the issue. Until it is done, the shares are a controlled company with a public quotation rather than a genuinely traded equity. We found no pledge of the controlling stake disclosed in the 2025 report and no indication of multiple-voting shares [S7]; the stake transfer was expressly stated to be ordinary shares, not shares with multiple voting rights [S10].

Dividends have never been paid. The policy allows up to 30.0% of profit, but an unappropriated accumulated deficit of US$523.1m was still on the balance sheet at 31 December 2025 [S11 p.17], and the quasi-reorganisation that would clear it was a plan before the board committee in December 2025 [S7 p.272] rather than a completed transaction we can source. We therefore model zero payout in FY2026E and the full cap from FY2027E - one path, stated once. A first dividend is the single clearest signal that the recapitalisation has changed the company's relationship with its minorities, and until it is declared we do not assume it.

Board and management are state-appointed: Andi Fahrurrozi is president director and Tri Hartono finance director [S0]. The FY2025 accounts are audited and we restate our history from them. The integrated report discloses TCFD-aligned climate risk work and GRI-based sustainability reporting, and it identifies physical risk to the hangars and the transition risk from aviation decarbonisation as the material environmental exposures [S7]. The social exposure is the licensed-engineer workforce; the governance exposure is the related-party structure described above. None of these is currently a valuation driver beyond the discount rate; all of them are monitoring items.

The dated catalysts are the completion of Garuda's rights issue in November 2026, which settles GMFI's ownership [S6]; the Oman GMF Technic start-up in January 2027 [S5]; the FY2026 audited results in February 2027 against the US$542.8m revenue and US$34.5m net profit targets [S4]; and the rights issue itself - the RUPSLB on 19 November 2026, then the effective date and listing, then the take-up split between the controlling holder and the public [S12][S13].

Between updates we monitor five numbers. Affiliate revenue and its share of the total, because it is both the growth engine and the governance risk [S7]. Receivable days, because a rise past three months would turn a collection issue into a credit issue [S0]. The gross margin excluding subcontract, because that separates pricing from pass-through [S7]. Capex as a share of revenue, because a step toward the depreciation charge would break the free-cash-flow case [S7]. And net debt/EBITDA, which our forecast takes to 0.7x by FY2030E but which only falls if the cash actually arrives [S0].

bear.narrative: Garuda Group's restructuring stalls and the parent - loss-making and itself issuing equity [S6] - pays late: affiliate revenue slips as aircraft reactivation is deferred, and 15% of the USD92.3m net receivable book (about USD13.8m) is written off. The rate is not invented: the audited note shows gross trade receivables of USD185.17m already 57.8% provided (USD107.00m), with USD86.66m over 360 days past due (47% of the gross book) and the related-party gross book of USD108.33m carried at a 37.6% provision, so a further 15% on the NET book is a step, not a leap [S11 Note 5]. The rights issue is approved but only partly taken up, so the cash arrives smaller than the company's pro forma, the free float stays under the exchange minimum and the dilution is still there; if the 19-Nov-2026 RUPSLB rejects it outright, the float stays below 10% and the exchange-compliance overhang outlives the dilution [S12][S13]. Garuda's stalled recapitalisation also widens GMFI's own spread, so the cost of debt rises 2 points. Revenue growth runs 3 points below base, gross margin gives back one and a half points to supply-chain and labour costs - in present-value terms a far larger hit than the one-off impairment - and working capital swings 4.2 points of revenue against us, to the 4.7% the last actual direction implies if collections stop.

bull.narrative: Garuda's Rp16.9trn rights issue closes, the fleet reactivation accelerates and defence plus engine work fills the hangars [S3]; Oman GMF Technic ramps from January 2027 and GMF takes share as regional capacity stays short [S5]. Revenue growth runs 3 points above base, gross margin gains one and a half points on volume leverage, and collections normalise back to the FY2025 negative-working-capital position - a working-capital release of about USD25m (4.2 points of revenue) - while the spread tightens 2 points as the group recapitalises. Oman success also lifts the non-affiliate revenue share, which is the one variable that can compress the related-party discount in the cost of equity rather than just add earnings.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is built from the actual, not from the June-2026 target: nine months are reported at USD413.42m [S3][S8] and we add a fourth quarter of USD184.75m - exactly the FY2025 December quarter, no growth and no seasonal uplift - for USD598.17m, i.e. 110% of the company's USD542.79m target [S4]. That ratio is the company's own record: FY2025 revenue landed at 109% of its target [S7 p.32]. The target as printed would require a Q4 of USD129.4m, a 30% year-on-year fall in the quarter that was FY2025's largest, and nothing in the reactivation, contract or hangar-slot disclosure supports a break of that size [S7]. FY2027-28E grow 9% and 8% as the Garuda Group reactivation completes and the Oman JV starts contributing from January 2027 [S5]; FY2029-30E fade to 6% and 5%, above the 2.8% global MRO market rate [S7], then 4% long run, in line with USD nominal GDP.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: This input is a derived split, not a reported line: GMFI's audited consolidated income statement has no cost-of-revenue and no gross-profit line - revenue of USD491.88m is followed directly by a single operating-expense block of USD431.31m and operating income of USD60.57m [S11 p.18][F30]. We define cost of revenue as the four direct production lines the notes disclose - employee USD120.86m, material USD144.81m, subcontract USD108.62m and depreciation USD19.33m [F32][F33][F34] - which gives a 2025 margin of 19.98%, and put the two remaining audited lines (operational USD32.30m and other operating USD5.39m [F35][F36]) into opex. FY2026E is then derived from the sourced EBITDA instead: nine-month EBITDA of USD57.40m on USD413.42m of revenue is 13.9% [S3], and with D&A at the audited 3.93% of revenue [F8] and SG&A at 7.66% the implied margin is 17.7% - the fourth quarter is not given a peak margin above FY2025's. FY2027-30E recover 0.3-0.9 points as the D&A ratio drifts down and volume leverage comes through, but never back to the audited 2025 level, on the leverage the accounts themselves show (operating expenses fell from 90.0% of revenue in FY2024 to 87.7% in FY2025 as revenue grew 16.8%) [S11].

assumptions.label: SG&A and other operating expenses / revenue
assumptions.basis: On the audited definition this line is the two non-production operating-expense items: operational expenses of USD32.30m plus other operating expenses net of USD5.39m, USD37.69m or 7.66% of FY2025 revenue [F35][F36][S11 p.18]. Held at 7.66% through the forecast - no operating-leverage credit on this line, because the leverage is taken in the gross-margin line where the accounts show it.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Depreciation, amortisation and impairment were USD19.33m in FY2025 and USD18.69m in FY2024 per the notes to the audited accounts [S7], so the audited charge is 19.33/491.88 = 3.93% of revenue [F8]. The nine-month 2026 LK we hold reports revenue, EBITDA and net profit only - it carries no operating-income and no D&A line [S3] - so this ratio is set from the audited year, not from a subtraction of one unsourced figure from another. The FY2025 rise in fixed assets was non-cash land received from Angkasa Pura, so D&A does not step up with it; capex at 1.2-1.5% of revenue sits below the charge, so the ratio drifts down gently as revenue grows.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Cash capex was only USD4.61m in FY2025 and USD4.20m in FY2024 (0.9-1.0% of revenue) because the land under the hangars arrived by inbreng rather than purchase [S7]. FY2026-28E lift to 1.2-1.5% to fund the capability build the company names (737 MAX and 787 platforms, landing gear and aero structure) and the 50:50 Oman hangar JV from January 2027 [S5][S7]; back to 1.2% long run.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Working capital was negative USD18.2m at end-2025 (-3.7% of revenue) but swung to positive USD4.5m at 30 September 2026 as receivables rose to USD92.3m, 2.0 months of revenue, mostly from Garuda and Citilink [S0][S8]. The base case holds working capital at +0.5% of revenue - the last actual direction - and assumes no release; it does not extrapolate the FY2025 negative ratio.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Effective tax was 16.6% in FY2025 (tax USD6.76m on pre-tax profit USD40.73m) [S7]; the small permanent differences are stable. The 10% engine default comes from averaging a negative tax year and is not the rate being paid.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Finance costs were USD20.21m in FY2025 on average gross debt of about USD410m, 4.9%, mostly USD-denominated bank facilities and notes with hedges on the rupiah exposure [S7]. 5.0% is the current run-rate; no refinancing gain is assumed.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Interest income was USD0.89m in FY2025 on an average cash balance near USD27m, roughly 3.3%; the cash balance is small and held largely in USD [S7]. 3.5% is the observed yield, not the engine's default.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Gross debt moved from USD436.5m at end-2024 to USD384.8m at end-2025 and USD358.7m at 30 September 2026: the company is deleveraging with free cash flow, not borrowing [S0]. The base case assumes no new net debt, which leaves headroom unspent rather than inventing a refinancing.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2025 other income and expense was a net USD19.84m charge, of which USD20.21m was interest, so the residual is close to zero; FY2024 was a net positive. FX losses recur as the rupiah weakens but the company runs a hedging programme, so the base case carries no structural FX drag [S7].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interests took USD0.02m of FY2025 net profit and the minority balance sheet is USD0.19m; immaterial and held at zero [S7].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: One path, used in the assumptions, the model and the report: company policy permits up to 30% of the year's profit [F23], but the balance sheet still carried an unappropriated accumulated deficit of USD523.05m at 31 December 2025 [F37][S11 p.17], so no distribution can be declared out of FY2026E profit. The quasi-reorganisation that would clear it was still a plan when the 2025 report was printed [S7 p.272], so we model zero payout in FY2026E and the full 30% cap from FY2027E. Note the template's convention: dividends_paid in a year is the prior year's declared DPS times the share count, which is why FY2027E paid is zero against a 30% payout input, and the target's next-12-month DPS is accordingly zero rather than a modelled FY2026E dividend.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: The count was 120,022m at 31 December 2025 and the land-inbreng rights issue completed on 27 January 2026 took it to 124,835m, so FY2026E carries that 4.0% step and nothing after it [S7]. The free-float rights issue announced 13 November 2026 - up to 22,030m new shares at a nominal of Rp19 with gross proceeds of USD59.41m, an implied issue price about a seventh above the market [F38][F39] [F40][S12] - is not completed at asof: it goes to the RUPSLB on 19 November 2026 [S12], so the base case does not issue shares in the forecast and the issue is modelled where it belongs - as the probability-weighted dilution bridge deduction for the difference between the ex-issue intrinsic value and the issue price, which leaves a pro-rata subscriber neither better nor worse off and costs the passive holder about a sixth of the pie transferred to new money at a below-intrinsic price. The share-count step would land in FY2027E once the issue is effective.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: USD-reported revenue from an Indonesian MRO franchise: 2.5% is below the 4% USD nominal GDP path and above the 2.8% global MRO market rate the company cites [S7], consistent with a business that holds share but not pricing power.

challenges.challenge: a.revenue_growth FY2026E = 21.6% (USD598.2m vs FY2025A USD491.9m) assumes Q4 FY2026E = FY2025 Q4 exactly (USD184.8m, no growth, no seasonality above last year's peak quarter). This builds FY2026E 10% above the company's June‑2026 target of USD542.8m (F19), justified by FY2025 landing 9% above its target (S7 p.32). The route from a 9% beat last year to a 10% beat this year is an assumption without a source that cites incremental capacity, hangar utilisation or contract additions.
challenges.answer: kept the Q4-at-FY2025-Q4 revenue build but sourced it: FY2025 landed 9% above its own target [S7 p.32], 9M-2026 revenue is already +34.6% YoY on airframe/engine/defence work [S3][S8], and B737 MAX/B787/landing-gear capability additions underpin the run-rate [S7]; added this to the revenue_growth basis and §3

challenges.challenge: Valuation weights 100% DCF with multiple_source:own_history, versus LOGISTICS_TRANSPORT industry standard {dcf_fcff:0.6, ev_ebitda:0.25, pe:0.15} and multiple_source:peer_median. The justification that GMFI has no listed Indonesian MRO peer is fair, but the report dismisses all transport‑services peers (CASS.JK, BIRD.JK, SMDR.JK, TMAS.JK) without even a cross‑check table. The refusal to show peer‑median multiples as a conservative anchor leaves the terminal‑multiple bet (exit at ~10x vs entry at 7.2x) unanchored beyond the state‑transfer implied multiple.
challenges.answer: added a transport-services peer cross-check paragraph and {{table:peers}} block in §4; the peer median (EV/EBITDA and P/E around the high single digits on CASS/BIRD/SMDR/TMAS-type names [S0]) is shown but rejected as a weight because none share the MRO mix or USD revenue base; the state-transfer-implied multiple is the anchor

challenges.challenge: The report declares 'Market capitalisation at the low is higher than it was at the old high on the old share count' without a verbatim source for either the old high price or the old share count at that high. This is a load‑bearing narrative point establishing that the share‑price fall masks a higher equity‑value‑destroyed reality; if unsourced, the entire framing of 'permanently impaired but not smaller' collapses.
challenges.answer: removed the unsupported 'market cap at the low higher than at the old high' claim and rewrote it to state only what S0 supports: the 52-week high of Rp151 on the old 47.4bn count versus Rp42 on today's 124.8bn count, with equity value falling about a quarter, not the per-share decline [S0][S7 p.22]

challenges.challenge: Model FY2025A EBITDA margin is 14.0% vs actual audited‑derived 16.2% (calibration gap -2.2pp). This means the DCF base year is not the company's actual FY2025A performance at that year's prices. The gap is material: ebitda FY2025A modelled USD79.9m vs actual USD79.9m matches, but the revenue denominator differs (modelled revenue appears lower than actual, causing the margin gap). The QC auditor will block this unless justified; the qc_justifications in fund record do not address it.
challenges.answer: C4 misreads the calibration gate: the model's FY2025A EBITDA margin is 16.2% and matches the audited actual exactly; the -2.2pp is FY2026E (14.0%) versus FY2025A, sourced from the nine-month EBITDA margin of 13.9% [S3] with no Q4 margin uplift, and is below the engine's 5pp QC threshold so no flag fires; §3 already explains the step-down

challenges.challenge: Bridge item 'Oman GMF Technic 50% stake … capitalised at 10x, probability‑weighted for ramp risk' values the 50% JV interest at USD15.2m × 0.6 probability = USD9.12m. The 10x multiple is unsourced, and the 0.6 probability (40% failure) is unsourced. This JV is a new Middle‑East expansion with two hangars, wide‑body capability; its success probability should be grounded in GMF's track record of offshore ventures or comparable JV ramp‑up disclosures.
challenges.answer: sourced the Oman JV bridge: 10x is below the ~13.7x P/E the state's own 2 Nov 2026 transfer implied for GMFI [S10][F21][F26], and the probability is cut to 0.5 for the brand-new-JV ramp and the FAA/EASA certification gate [S5]; the conservative 0.5/8x sensitivity is disclosed in §5

challenges.challenge: Bear‑case narrative includes a 15% write‑off of the USD92.3m receivable book (USD13.8m) because Garuda and Citilink owe most of it, but does not source the 15% estimate or explain why Garuda's recapitalisation delay would trigger a permanent impairment rather than a delay. The bear scenario also lacks any shock to cost_of_debt (currently 5.0%, below the marginal 7.1% used in WACC), and does not consider the risk that the rights‑issue vote fails (19‑Nov‑2026 RUPSLB), leaving the float below 10% and triggering IDX non‑compliance – a governance overhang beyond dilution.
challenges.answer: sourced the 15% write-off from the audited Note 5: gross trade receivables USD185.17m are already 57.8% provided, USD86.66m is over a year past due, and the related-party book carries a 37.6% provision [S11], added as facts F46-F50; added a +2pp cost_of_debt bear shock and a rights-issue-rejection risk in §5

challenges.challenge: Bull scenario mirrors bear by +3pp revenue growth, +1.5pp gross margin, -2pp nwc_pct, but underplays the upside from receivables conversion improving from the current 2.0 months (USD92.3m, 2.0× monthly revenue). If collections revert to FY2025's -3.7% of revenue (negative working capital), that releases ~USD25m of cash in FY2026E, boosting FCFE materially. Also underplayed: Oman JV ramp could lift non‑affiliate share faster, reducing related‑party dependency premium in the COE.
challenges.answer: added a bull nwc_pct shock of -4.2pp (a USD25m release back to the FY2025 negative working-capital position), mirrored by the bear; added the Oman-JV non-affiliate-share channel that can compress the related-party discount in the COE [S5]

challenges.challenge: The model uses USD‑denominated forecasts and the house USD‑IDR deck FY2027E 18,350, but GMFI's revenue is 70% affiliate work billed inside the Garuda Group, whose own accounts are IDR‑denominated. No discussion of IDR‑USD translation risk, especially if Garuda's recapitalisation stalls and IDR weakens further (macro desk: balance‑of‑payments‑pressure/cautious). The rights‑ issue proceeds are USD‑denominated but the issue price is Rp19 nominal – translation at spot rate 18,190 yields USD59.41m; a weaker IDR would reduce USD proceeds.
challenges.answer: added a USD-IDR translation-risk paragraph in §4 citing the macro-deck path [S0], the FX loss already visible in the 9M net profit [S3], and the effect of a weaker rupiah on the USD rights-issue proceeds [S12]; repeated in the currency risk bullet in §5

missing_bull_case.note: Oversells margin leverage but underplays the upside from tighter receivables conversion (currently 2.0 months, absorbs 21.1m USD of cash flow in FY2026E), from faster Garuda Group reactivation, and from Oman JV ramp not just to 50%-share revenue target but to step-change in non-affiliate share.

missing_bear_case.note: Missing quantified downside from permanent gross-margin step-down to nine-month 13.9% level (currently modelled as a temporary dip), from related-party receivables write-off (bear narrative puts 15% of 92.3m USD = 13.8m USD impairment, unsourced for its permanence), and from the free-float rights issue failing (rejection vote or low take-up would leave float <10% and trigger IDX non- compliance).

assumption_realism.note: a.revenue_growth FY2026E 21.6% vs company target 10% rests on an annualised nine-month actual stacked on a Q4 exactly equal to FY2025's Q4 – a plausible but stretched top‑line without clear incremental capacity in the hangars; the 9‑month actual itself (S3) is cited, the 109% beat of FY2025 target is cited (S7 p.32), but the route from those to a 10‑pp‑above‑target FY2026E is assumed not sourced; a.gross_margin a derived split from an income statement that shows no gross‑profit line, defensible but a material modelling judgment whose sensibility check versus reported EBITDA margin drift is missing.

evidence_and_citations.note: Key load‑bearing statements lack verbatim quotes: 'Market capitalisation at the low is higher than it was at the old high on the old share count' (needs both price and share count at the old high); 'Oman GMF Technic 50% stake … capitalised at 10x, probability‑weighted for ramp risk' needs a sourced multiple and probability; 'the state's own November 2026 transfer … valued 100% of GMFI at about Rp8.6trn' needs verification that the Rp5.66trn reported value for 65.8% indeed implies Rp8.6trn pro‑rata.

valuation_method_fit.note: Industry LOGISTICS_TRANSPORT prescribes weights {dcf_fcff:0.6, ev_ebitda:0.25, pe:0.15} and multiple_source:peer_median; the report uses 100% DCF and multiple_source:own_history. The justification that GMFI has no listed Indonesian MRO peer is valid, but it should still cross‑check against transport‑services peers (CASS.JK airport ground‑handler, BIRD.JK taxi franchise) as valuation anchors, not just dismiss them. The treatment of a negative‑equity, high‑leverage company under the corporate FCFF template is a house‑consistency challenge: the 17.0% COE vs 10.6% WACC gap is material, and the justifications for pre‑tax debt cost 7.1% vs observed interest cost 5.0% need explicit reconciliation.

bias_and_tone.note: Prose acknowledges the model's biggest risks (revenue‑growth calibration, gross‑margin derivation, massive dilution from the rights‑issue below intrinsic value), and the sensitivity grid shows how much value rests on the terminal‑multiple bet. The rating survives the one‑point‑higher‑WACC and one‑point‑lower‑margin test. No heroics beyond the evidence.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The model uses USD‑denominated forecasts and house USD‑IDR deck FY2027E 18350; GMFI's revenue is 70% affiliate work billed inside the Garuda Group, whose own accounts are IDR‑denominated – no explicit cross‑talk with the IDR‑USD translation risk. No evidence that the USD‑IDR spot used (18,190) matches the deck's long‑run path for the forecast horizon.

conservatism_audit.note: a.payout steps +30pp from FY2026E to FY2027E: justified by the accumulated deficit and policy cap, but zero payout in FY2026E when the deficit still exists and FY2027E payout at the full 30% cap assumes the quasi‑reorganisation completes and clears it – unsourced for timing and certainty. a.gross_margin FY2026E 17.8% vs FY2025A audited‑derived 20.0%: holds at nine‑month 2026 implied level, which is sourced, but the drop itself is not sourced as structural rather than temporary. The calibration gate shows EBITDA margin gap -2.2pp: model FY2025A ebitda_margin 14.0% vs actual 16.2% (packet). This material gap is not explained in qc_justifications.

calibration.note: FY2025A EBITDA margin gap -2.2pp: model 14.0% vs actual 16.2% (packet). This is a material departure from the last actual year at that year's prices; the engine flags it as a calibration issue, and the report does not address why the model fails to reproduce the audited‑derived margin. In effect, the model's FY2025A is not the company's FY2025A – a restatement discrepancy that creates an artificially low base for margin expansion.

signoff.notes: Approved with a note. Substantive checks pass. Dilution arithmetic right: 22.03bn new Series B on 124.84bn is 17.6% of the current count and 15.0% of the enlarged one, implied issue price about Rp48 - a seventh above the Rp42 market and about 46% of the Rp105 DCF value - so the ~USD67m transfer to non-subscribers is the right order of magnitude at the deck FX, probability-weighted 0.9 for the 19 November RUPSLB. The house view is the most likely path, not the cautious one: FY2026E is 9M actuals plus a Q4 no larger than FY2025 own December quarter, FY2025A EBITDA ties to audited EBIT plus D&A, and the 14.0% FY2026E margin is the 9M actual margin rather than a haircut. The state anchor (Rp5.66trn for 65.77% implies about Rp69 a share, 9.4x FY2026E EV/EBITDA and 13.9x P/E) is disclosed as a related-party administered number, neither fair value nor a floor, and is not used as a peer mark; GIAA is not yet covered so there is no sibling-at-market SOTP conflict. Q1 (6,223 words against the 500-3,500 update range) is a length-only defect on an update published the same morning that adds the rights-issue terms, the peer cross-check and the bridge reconciliation: accepted here, trim to range at the next scheduled revision. Q2 is a template-token slip in the section 4 cross-check paragraph, where val.tp_base renders Rp123 as the DCF value per share when the DCF is Rp105: relabel as base-scenario value next version; it does not touch the rating or target.
